clue.text: English rock band, once big in the East?

definitions.meaning: a supergroup formed in 1981 whose debut album topped the US charts
the eastern part of the world, the Orient

explanation.surface: A wistful question about a British band that used to be famous in eastern countries.
explanation.walkthrough: The band takes its name from the continent, so the one word answers both halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The continent is what Westerners have long called the East or the Orient, and the band shares its name.

clue.text: Bloke playing old fashionable instrument

parts.note: a bloke is a man

indicators.note: playing about with the letters of the word old rearranges them

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing

explanation.surface: A man strumming an old-fashioned instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old fashionable' reads as 'old-fashioned', but 'playing' scrambles OLD to DOL and 'fashionable' is IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A lute-like stringed instrument with paired strings, plucked with a plectrum.

clue.text: Wife's present: divorcing husband at one time past

indicators.note: divorcing separates a partner off, so the husband's letter is parted from the word

parts.note: here means present, in attendance

explanation.surface: A wife's present to herself on divorce: the husband is a thing of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the plural past tense of 'to be', describing what existed at one time gone by.

clue.text: Punishment for most of this cake being spongy, right?

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is used
spongy suggests something soft and pliable, so the letters of cake are squashed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is being punished for baking a cake that turned out spongy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being spongy' gives CKEA; 'most of' drops the last letter of 'this'. A thick ear is a cuff round the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip round the ear given as old-fashioned British chastisement, especially of children.

clue.text: Conservative leader to suffer defeat? Time for recess

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: to lose is to suffer defeat

explanation.surface: A Conservative Party leader loses an election and is sent off to the backbenches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recess' looks like a parliamentary break, but here it is a nook in a room.
explanation.definitionFit: A small cupboard or enclosed nook set into a wall is a type of recess.

clue.text: £1,000 at first, young learner's car reverses, collecting debts kindly

indicators.note: at first places this piece at the front of the answer

parts.note: G, short for a grand, is slang for a thousand pounds

indicators.note: collecting takes something in, so the debts go inside the reversed letters
reverses means the young learner's car is written backwards

parts.note: L is the learner sign on a British car
taken as written
IOUs are written promises to pay, so debts

explanation.surface: A learner driver reverses a car worth a thousand pounds while a debt collector looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' gives RACLY; 'collecting' puts the debts inside it, after its third letter. G for a grand is slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting graciously means acting with courtesy and kindness, so the two adverbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Seeks these at Wimbledon

definitions.meaning: woos or pursues, as a suitor seeks someone's affection
the grass playing areas at the London tennis championships

explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the verb of wooing, the other the tennis playing surfaces.
explanation.definitionFit: To woo someone is to pursue their affection; also, tennis is played on marked rectangular playing areas.

clue.text: Ground lies surrounded by water

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase describing a piece of land; the answer is the noun for such land

indicators.note: ground in the sense of crushed or milled, so the letters of lies are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Lies are told about land surrounded by water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a noun meaning land, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island is land that has water all around it.

clue.text: He's ripped on the outside, one very trim

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit on the outside, wrapping round the other piece
ripped means torn apart, so the letters of He's are reassembled

parts.note: A means one, as in a single item

explanation.surface: A ripped man who keeps himself very trim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ripped' makes SHE from HE'S, which goes round A and V.
explanation.definitionFit: A trim is a light cut of hair, and a close cut of the beard is a similar grooming act.

clue.text: Liberal wearing tousled hair promises to be funny

indicators.note: the scrambled hair is worn by the Liberal, so it encloses that letter
tousled hair is messed up, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician with messy hair promises to be entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tousled' gives HIAR, and 'wearing' has it put on round the Liberal's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extremely amusing is very funny; the two words are close synonyms.

clue.text: Car seen racing over 100 by groups of spectators

parts.note: Audi is a German car make

indicators.note: the racing letters go over the hundred, covering it
racing suggests rushing around, so the letters of seen are mixed

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A car spotted racing at over 100 by crowds watching a motor race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racing' gives ENES, which 'over' wraps round the hundred to make ENCES.
explanation.definitionFit: Crowds gathered to watch or listen to a performance are audiences.

clue.text: Swear at dog, tips of sausages eaten

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog

indicators.note: the tips of words are their starting letters here

explanation.surface: Someone swears at the dog that has eaten the sausages.
explanation.definitionFit: To damn someone with oaths is to swear at them, the verb sense of profane abuse.

clue.text: Scottish hero — an expert climber?

definitions.meaning: William ..., leader in the Scottish Wars of Independence
read whimsically as ..., someone brilliant at scaling walls

explanation.walkthrough: Split the name into WALL and ACE for the second, whimsical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wallace led Scotland against England; split in two the name reads as a champion of walls.

clue.text: Grown apart, as not suitable

indicators.note: apart means broken into pieces, so the letters of Grown are rearranged

explanation.surface: A couple who have grown apart are no longer right for each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inappropriate or improper for an occasion is the wrong thing, not fit for it.

clue.text: English author, one left in river with powerboats?

parts.note: A means one

indicators.note: in places the letter for left inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
split as power + boats: P for power and arks for boats

explanation.surface: An English writer, one who left for a river trip with powerboats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'powerboats' must be split: P (power) and ARKS (boats).
explanation.definitionFit: Adele Parks is a bestselling English novelist of contemporary fiction.

clue.text: Pocket for everyone in Eastbourne, say, in retirement

indicators.note: in puts the letter for everyone inside the reversed word
retiring means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Eastbourne is a seaside resort on England's south coast
U is the film rating for universal, suitable for everyone

explanation.surface: Pensioners in retirement in Eastbourne pocket something for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retirement' turns RESORT into TROSER, with U inside. EASTBOURNE is a south-coast English seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser money is British slang for taking it for oneself, putting it in one's pocket.

clue.text: Mature writing with Apple device?

parts.note: R stands for writing, one of the three Rs of reading, writing and arithmetic
Apple names gadgets with an i- prefix, so a fanciful Apple pen would be an iPen

explanation.surface: A grown-up writing with a gadget made by Apple.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the Apple device is invented on the pattern of iPod and iPad.
explanation.definitionFit: To mature is to grow fully developed, as fruit does when it ripens.

clue.text: Cat in the past goes round the bend

indicators.note: goes round means one piece encircles the other

parts.note: once means formerly, in the past
a U-bend is shaped like the letter U

explanation.surface: A cat that used to be sane has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round the bend' looks like the idiom for mad, but the bend is the U shape.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow leopard is also called by this name, a large wild feline of Central Asia.

clue.text: Manage to exercise

definitions.meaning: to manage a business is to direct it
to jog or go out at pace for fitness

explanation.definitionFit: To be in charge of a shop is to operate it; going for a jog is a form of exercise.

clue.text: Writers' blocks

parts.note: writer's block is an inability to write; here the blocks are pads of paper that writers use

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests writer's block, the loss of inspiration, but it means literal blocks of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Glued stacks of tear-off paper sheets are blocks that writers jot on.

clue.text: Animal urinates over top of hedge, facing the other way

indicators.note: facing the other way turns the letters to run backwards
the urinating word sits over the letter, enclosing it

parts.note: pees means urinates

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An animal relieves itself over a hedge, then turns round.
explanation.walkthrough: PEES around H gives PEEHS; 'facing the other way' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A woolly farm ruminant raised for meat and fleece is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Outside bird caged by old metal

indicators.note: the bird is caged, so it sits inside the other letters

parts.note: ex means former, so old
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A bird outside, kept in an old metal cage.
explanation.definitionFit: External and outside both describe the exterior part of something; they are synonyms.

clue.text: Plots involve danger close to Paris

indicators.note: involve in its old sense of roll up or entangle, so the letters of danger are wound into a new order
the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Conspiracies near Paris put people in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plots' suggests schemes, but it means pieces of land.
explanation.definitionFit: Plots of cultivated ground are gardens or allotments, areas where plants are grown.

clue.text: Talk with pet

definitions.meaning: British slang for chatter at length
a long-eared animal kept at home

explanation.walkthrough: To 'rabbit on' is British slang for talking endlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom 'rabbit on' means to chatter; the long-eared animal is a common household pet.

clue.text: Old queen is turning brown

indicators.note: turning means the letters are spun round to read backwards

parts.note: Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly queen is going brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses ANNE IS to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw or burnt sienna is an earthy pigment of yellowish or reddish brown shade.

clue.text: Moon about end of party, to act audaciously

indicators.note: about means around, so the moon's letters surround the other one

parts.note: Triton is the largest moon of Neptune

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Mooning about at the end of a party is a cheeky thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moon' looks like a verb, mope, but it is Neptune's satellite.
explanation.definitionFit: This British idiom means to chance one's arm, testing how much one can get away with.

clue.text: Mathematical symbol displayed on a blackboard

indicators.note: displayed means the letters are shown within the run of the clue words

explanation.surface: A mathematical symbol written up on a blackboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The inverted triangle used in vector calculus for the del operator is this mathematical symbol.

clue.text: Cocaine stolen by family returning to prison

indicators.note: something stolen is taken in, so the family letters hold the drug
returning means the word family's synonym is read backwards

parts.note: kin are family
C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: Cocaine stolen by a family who are going back to jail.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses this word for a police station or jail, a sense of prison.

clue.text: Authorised captive queen to be dropped into English sea

indicators.note: the captive and queen are dropped inside the sea's letters

parts.note: the Med is the Mediterranean Sea
POW, prisoner of war, is a captive
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone authorised a captured queen to be dumped in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Being empowered means being given authority or official power to act.

clue.text: Woman has dirty laundry

indicators.note: dirty suggests muddied, so the letters of has are messed up

explanation.surface: A woman has a pile of dirty laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes collected to be cleaned together are the weekly wash, a load of laundry.

clue.text: American's sci-fi novel under construction: centre of Earth is missing!

definitions.note: Frank Herbert, an American writer, wrote this 1965 desert-planet epic

indicators.note: construction means building up anew, so the letters of under are rearranged
the centre of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: An American sci-fi novel is being written, but the plot's Earth-core idea is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is missing' says the R from Earth's centre is the letter left over when UNDER is rebuilt.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Herbert's 1965 novel set on the desert planet Arrakis is a landmark of science fiction.

clue.text: To have shown fear in checked pants

indicators.note: pants as British slang for rubbish, so the letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone scared while wearing checked trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' reads as trousers but signals the anagram. In British slang 'pants' also means rubbish or poor.
explanation.definitionFit: To chicken out is to back away through cowardice, so this past form means lost one's nerve.

clue.text: Country's at home beyond spring

indicators.note: beyond places the home piece after the spring

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring
in means at home

explanation.surface: A country retreat beyond a hot spring.
explanation.definitionFit: A country on the Iberian peninsula in south-west Europe.
